title: Sentinel-Controlled Loops
learningObjectives: Explain sentinel values as input termination signals.
Exclude sentinel from processing and totals.
Handle empty data sets and zero counts.
Guard extraction failures in input loops.
Use sentinels when input length is not known in advance.

understand.concept: A sentinel is a special input value that ends processing. Check it before treating the value as ordinary data; also handle failed input extraction.
understand.whyItMatters: Sentinel loops handle unknown input counts without requiring a separate length.
understand.explain: Read, check sentinel, process, then read again. Guard empty totals before calculating averages.

examples.title: Sum until -1
examples.explanation: Sentinel is tested before summing; add stream-failure handling for robustness.

examples.title: Count until zero
examples.explanation: Zero ends entry and is not counted.

examples.title: Sentinel with break
examples.explanation: Exit command is not processed as normal data.

examples.title: Extraction-safe condition
examples.explanation: Failed extraction and sentinel both stop processing.

practise.guidedTask: For Sentinel-Controlled Loops, trace each example in a table showing the loop's initial state, condition result, body action, update step, and final state. Identify the termination point and boundary behavior.
practise.independentTask: Write a small C++ exercise focused on Sentinel-Controlled Loops. Include at least three test cases (typical, boundary and termination/invalid-input case where relevant), trace the loop iterations, and explain why it stops or skips/continues as intended.
hints: Write down the loop's starting state.
Trace the condition before/after each pass according to loop type.
Check that every continuing path progresses toward termination.
Test boundary values and early-exit paths.
Count passes explicitly to catch off-by-one errors.

questions.explanation: Sentinel signals that input is finished.
No ordinary values means count zero.
